claim: Wnt1-Cre mice drive Cre-dependent transgene expression in neural crest derivatives, which include Schwann cells.
source: Wnt1-Cre mice drive Cre-dependent transgene expression in neural crest derivatives, which include Schwann cells (Danielian et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Danielian et al., 1998, which provides published evidence for this statement.

claim: Robust expression of TdTomato was observed at early ages in all Schwann cells in the diaphragm, including myelinating Schwann cells of the phrenic nerve as well as non-myelinating TPSCs at the NMJ.
source: Robust expression of TdTomato was observed at early ages in all Schwann cells in the diaphragm, including myelinating Schwann cells of the phrenic nerve as well as non-myelinating TPSCs at the NMJ (Figure 1A), visualized using fluorescent α−bungarotoxin (α-BTX).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 1A showing TdTomato expression in Schwann cells.

claim: GCaMP3 is expressed in all TPSCs of P7 diaphragm in Wnt1-GCaMP3 mice.
source: In whole-mounts of P7 diaphragm muscle incubated with GFP antibodies to label GCaMP3, S100 antibodies to detect Schwann cells, and α-BTX to visualize NMJs, we observed expression of GCaMP3 in all TPSCs (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data showing GCaMP3 expression in TPSCs, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Wnt1-Cre drives robust expression of GCaMP3 in TPSCs of the early postnatal diaphragm.
source: Together, these results show that Wnt1-Cre drives robust expression of GCaMP3 in TPSCs of the early postnatal diaphragm.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in the preceding text and figures.

claim: Large populations of TPSCs respond to 45 s of 40 Hz tonic phrenic nerve stimulation.
source: Imaging these responses before and after nerve stimulation at low magnification (20X), we observed large populations of TPSCs that responded to 45 s of 40 Hz tonic phrenic nerve stimulation (Figure 2A; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing TPSC responses to nerve stimulation, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Each individual TPSC responds to high-frequency stimulation (HFS).
source: Higher magnification images (60X) showed that each individual TPSC, identified by labeling with fluorescent α-BTX (data not shown), responded to HFS (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-magnification imaging data showing individual TPSC responses, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The onset of Ca2+ transients in TPSCs occurs 1.8 ± 0.74 s after the initiation of HFS.
source: The onset of these transients occurred 1.8 ± 0.74 s (n = 5, c = 54) after the initiation of HFS, reached peak intensity at 2.86 ± 0.49 s after the onset of the transient, and shortly thereafter declined in amplitude (time to 50% decay = 13.35 ± 4.22 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient kinetics from imaging data.

claim: Ca2+ transients in TPSCs reach peak intensity at 2.86 ± 0.49 s after the onset of the transient.
source: The onset of these transients occurred 1.8 ± 0.74 s (n = 5, c = 54) after the initiation of HFS, reached peak intensity at 2.86 ± 0.49 s after the onset of the transient, and shortly thereafter declined in amplitude (time to 50% decay = 13.35 ± 4.22 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient kinetics from imaging data.

claim: The time to 50% decay of Ca2+ transients in TPSCs is 13.35 ± 4.22 s.
source: The onset of these transients occurred 1.8 ± 0.74 s (n = 5, c = 54) after the initiation of HFS, reached peak intensity at 2.86 ± 0.49 s after the onset of the transient, and shortly thereafter declined in amplitude (time to 50% decay = 13.35 ± 4.22 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient kinetics from imaging data.

claim: GCaMP3-expressing TPSCs respond to multiple stimulations.
source: GCaMP3-expressing TPSCs responded to multiple stimulations, providing a useful tool to measure the effects of different stimuli on the same TPSCs.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of repeated stimulation responses.

claim: The peak intensity of Ca2+ transients after a second bout of 40 Hz stimulation is lower than that of the first.
source: Similar to a previous study (Darabid et al., 2013), the peak intensity of Ca2+ transients observed after a subsequent 45 s bout of 40 Hz stimulation was lower than that of the first (17.3 ± 2.5 vs. 13.3 ± 1.1 dB, first vs. second stim, n = 5; p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing first and second stimulation responses, and is consistent with a previous study (Darabid et al., 2013).

claim: There is substantial variability in the onset of Ca2+ transients in TPSCs across large regions of the diaphragm after nerve stimulation (from 0.8 s to 4.3 s).
source: Interestingly, analyses of transients in TPSCs across large regions of the diaphragm from low-magnification videos showed substantial variability in the onset after nerve stimulation (from 0.8 s to 4.3 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of calcium imaging data from low-magnification videos.

claim: Individual muscle fibers across the entire diaphragm exhibit shortening at nearly the same onset after nerve stimulation.
source: Because individual muscle fibers across the entire diaphragm exhibit shortening at nearly the same onset after nerve stimulation (Figure 2—video 1), this result does not appear to result from differential transmitter release.
evidence: The claim is supported by video analysis of muscle fiber shortening, as shown in Figure 2—video 1.

claim: The variability in onset of TPSC Ca2+ transients does not result from differential transmitter release.
source: Because individual muscle fibers across the entire diaphragm exhibit shortening at nearly the same onset after nerve stimulation (Figure 2—video 1), this result does not appear to result from differential transmitter release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that muscle fibers contract synchronously despite variable TPSC Ca2+ onset times.

claim: The duration of TPSC Ca2+ transients is longer in response to 45 s of 40 Hz phasic vs. tonic stimulation.
source: The duration of TPSC Ca2+ transients was longer in response to 45 s of 40 Hz phasic vs. tonic stimulation (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of calcium transient durations under different stimulation patterns, as shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Peak transient intensities in response to 40 Hz tonic vs. phasic stimulation are statistically non-significant (14.7 ± 0.4 vs. 13.5 ± 1.3 dB; p=0.21; n = 3; c = 18).
source: Peak transient intensities were statistically non-significant (14.7 ± 0.4 vs. 13.5 ± 1.3 dB; p=0.21; n = 3; c = 18), and duration was longer (time to 50% decay = 15.4 ± 0.7 vs. 22.3 ± 3.7 s; p<0.05) in response to phasic vs. tonic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium transient peak intensities under different stimulation patterns.

claim: Duration of Ca2+ transients is longer (time to 50% decay = 15.4 ± 0.7 vs. 22.3 ± 3.7 s; p<0.05) in response to phasic vs. tonic stimulation.
source: Peak transient intensities were statistically non-significant (14.7 ± 0.4 vs. 13.5 ± 1.3 dB; p=0.21; n = 3; c = 18), and duration was longer (time to 50% decay = 15.4 ± 0.7 vs. 22.3 ± 3.7 s; p<0.05) in response to phasic vs. tonic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium transient durations under different stimulation patterns.

claim: The off-period of each duty cycle can be discerned as a dropoff in transient intensity during phasic stimulation.
source: The off-period of each duty cycle could clearly be discerned as a dropoff in transient intensity (Figure 2E), showing the dynamic nature of these responses (Todd et al., 2010; Darabid et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual analysis of calcium transients during phasic stimulation, as shown in Figure 2E, and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Ca2+ transients in response to 10 Hz stimulation are much slower in onset after nerve stimulation than after 40 Hz stimulation.
source: Interestingly, in response to 10 Hz stimulation, the lowest phasic rate that produced a measurable response, Ca2+ transients were much slower in onset after nerve stimulation than after 40 Hz stimulation (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of calcium transient onset times at different stimulation frequencies, as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Spontaneous ACh release, 1 Hz and 2 Hz evoked stimulation fail to produce visible Ca2+ transients in TPSCs.
source: Whereas spontaneous ACh release, 1 Hz and 2 Hz evoked stimulation failed to produce visible Ca2+ transients in TPSCs, 5 Hz stimulation elicited transients in a small number of TPSCs, and 10–40 Hz stimulation produced responses in all TPSCs (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of TPSC responses to different stimulation frequencies.

claim: 5 Hz stimulation elicits Ca2+ transients in a small number of TPSCs.
source: Whereas spontaneous ACh release, 1 Hz and 2 Hz evoked stimulation failed to produce visible Ca2+ transients in TPSCs, 5 Hz stimulation elicited transients in a small number of TPSCs, and 10–40 Hz stimulation produced responses in all TPSCs (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of TPSC responses to different stimulation frequencies.

claim: 10–40 Hz stimulation produces Ca2+ responses in all TPSCs.
source: Whereas spontaneous ACh release, 1 Hz and 2 Hz evoked stimulation failed to produce visible Ca2+ transients in TPSCs, 5 Hz stimulation elicited transients in a small number of TPSCs, and 10–40 Hz stimulation produced responses in all TPSCs (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of TPSC responses to different stimulation frequencies.

claim: Only several TPSCs respond to 0.1 s of 40 Hz nerve stimulation (i.e., four pulses).
source: In response to different durations of 40 Hz stimulation, only several TPSCs responded to 0.1 s of nerve stimulation (i.e., four pulses), whereas all TPSCs responded to 1–30 s of 40 Hz stimulation (Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of TPSC responses to different stimulation durations, as shown in Figure 2—video 2.

claim: All TPSCs respond to 1–30 s of 40 Hz stimulation.
source: In response to different durations of 40 Hz stimulation, only several TPSCs responded to 0.1 s of nerve stimulation (i.e., four pulses), whereas all TPSCs responded to 1–30 s of 40 Hz stimulation (Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of TPSC responses to different stimulation durations, as shown in Figure 2—video 2.

claim: Myelinating Schwann cells along phrenic nerve trunks and branches fail to exhibit Ca2+ responses to nerve stimulation.
source: Finally, in contrast to TPSCs, myelinating Schwann cells along phrenic nerve trunks and branches failed to exhibit Ca2+ responses, similar to previous reports (Jahromi et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and is consistent with previous reports (Jahromi et al., 1992).

claim: Bath application of ATP or muscarine elicits a Ca2+ response in Schwann cells along distal phrenic nerve branches as well as TPSCs.
source: However, bath application of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) or muscarine elicited a response in Schwann cells along distal phrenic nerve branches as well as TPSCs (Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of Schwann cell responses to drug application, as shown in Figure 2—video 3.

claim: Myelinating Schwann cells along larger phrenic nerve branches fail to respond to either nerve stimulation or bath application of ATP or muscarine.
source: Despite their expression of GCaMP3 (determined by immunohistochemistry; data not shown), myelinating Schwann cells along larger phrenic nerve branches failed to respond to either nerve stimulation or bath application of ATP or muscarine.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of myelinating Schwann cell responses.

claim: TPSCs dynamically respond to different patterns of neuronal activity.
source: Together, these results show that TPSCs dynamically respond to different patterns of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in the preceding text.

claim: A variety of neurotransmitter-derived substances trigger cytosolic Ca2+ accumulation in TPSCs, including ACh through muscarinic AChRs, adenine nucleotides such as ATP/ADP through purinergic P2Y receptors (P2YR), and adenosine through P1R.
source: Previous studies of individual or small cohorts of TPSCs show that a variety of neurotransmitter-derived substances trigger cytosolic Ca2+ accumulation, including ACh through muscarinic AChRs, adenine nucleotides such as ATP/ADP through purinergic P2Y receptors (P2YR), and adenosine, derived from synaptic ectonucleotidase-mediated degradation of adenine nucleotides (Cunha et al., 1996), through P1R (Darabid et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cunha et al., 1996; Darabid et al., 2014).

claim: TPSCs respond to nerve-derived ACh through nicotinic AChRs.
source: A recent study provided evidence that TPSCs also respond to nerve-derived ACh through nicotinic AChRs (Petrov et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Petrov et al., 2014).

claim: TPSC Ca2+ signals in neonatal mouse soleus are not mediated by muscarinic or nicotinic ACh receptor or by adenosine receptor activation, but rather by P2YRs.
source: In contrast to these responses in adult TPSCs, a recent report demonstarted that TPSC Ca2+ signals in neonatal mouse soleus are not mediated by muscarinic or nicotinic ACh receptor (mAChR) or by adenosine receptor activation, but rather by P2YRs (Darabid et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent report (Darabid et al., 2013).

claim: The pan-muscarinic antagonist atropine and the pan-nicotinic antagonist curare fail to block activity-mediated Ca2+ transients in TPSCs of the P7 diaphragm.
source: In agreement with this finding, we found that whereas the pan-muscarinic antagonist atropine and the pan-nicotinic antagonist curare failed to block activity-mediated Ca2+ transients in TPSCs of the P7 diaphragm (n = 8), the wide spectrum P2 antagonist suramin completely eliminated them (n = 6; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments showing lack of effect of atropine and curare, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The wide spectrum P2 antagonist suramin completely eliminates activity-mediated Ca2+ transients in TPSCs of the P7 diaphragm.
source: In agreement with this finding, we found that whereas the pan-muscarinic antagonist atropine and the pan-nicotinic antagonist curare failed to block activity-mediated Ca2+ transients in TPSCs of the P7 diaphragm (n = 8), the wide spectrum P2 antagonist suramin completely eliminated them (n = 6; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments showing complete blockade by suramin, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TPSCs express P2Y1 receptors.
source: We tested whether this response was mediated by P2Y1 receptors (P2Y1Rs), as TPSCs reportedly express this protein (Darabid et al., 2013) and astrocytic Ca2+ signaling is mediated in part by the Gq GPCR-coupled pathway that is activated by P2Y1Rs (Fam et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Darabid et al., 2013; Fam et al., 2000).

claim: Astrocytic Ca2+ signaling is mediated in part by the Gq GPCR-coupled pathway that is activated by P2Y1Rs.
source: We tested whether this response was mediated by P2Y1 receptors (P2Y1Rs), as TPSCs reportedly express this protein (Darabid et al., 2013) and astrocytic Ca2+ signaling is mediated in part by the Gq GPCR-coupled pathway that is activated by P2Y1Rs (Fam et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Fam et al., 2000).

claim: Treatment with the selective P2Y1R antagonist MRS2500 (1 μM) completely blocks activity-induced Ca2+ responses in all TPSCs of the diaphragm.
source: Treatment with the selective P2Y1R antagonist MRS2500 (1 μM) completely blocked activity-induced Ca2+ responses in all TPSCs of the diaphragm (n = 5; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments showing complete blockade by MRS2500, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Activity-dependent, P2Y1R-mediated Ca2+ responses in TPSCs are dependent on release from intracellular stores.
source: In order to determine whether activity-dependent, P2Y1R-mediated Ca2+ responses were dependent on release from intracellular stores, we examined them in the presence of the sarco-/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) inhibitor cyclopiazonic acid (CPA). 15 min after treatment with CPA, these responses were completely abolished (n = 3; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments showing abolishment of responses by the SERCA inhibitor CPA, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Nerve stimulation of P2ry1 mutants completely fails to elicit Ca2+ responses in TPSCs.
source: Finally, to test whether the effect of MRS2500 was indeed mediated by P2Y1Rs, we crossed mice expressing a constitutive null mutation of the P2ry1 gene, which encodes P2Y1Rs (Fabre et al., 1999), to Wnt1-GCaMP3 mice. Nerve stimulation of P2ry1 mutants completely failed to elicit Ca2+ responses in TPSCs (n = 7; Figure 3A,C; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic experiments using P2ry1 mutant mice, as shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: P2ry1 mutant TPSCs exhibit a robust response to muscarine.
source: Mutant TPSCs exhibited a robust response to muscarine (Figure 3A,C), indicating that the failure of activity to induce these responses was not caused by non-specific effects of the P2ry1 mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing muscarine-induced responses in P2ry1 mutant TPSCs, as shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: The failure of activity to induce Ca2+ responses in P2ry1 mutant TPSCs is not caused by non-specific effects of the P2ry1 mutation.
source: Mutant TPSCs exhibited a robust response to muscarine (Figure 3A,C), indicating that the failure of activity to induce these responses was not caused by non-specific effects of the P2ry1 mutation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that P2ry1 mutant TPSCs can still respond to muscarine.

claim: Atropine largely blocks muscarine-induced, but not nerve stimulation-induced, TPSC Ca2+ responses.
source: Atropine largely blocks muscarine-induced, but not nerve stimulation-induced, TPSC Ca2+ responses.
evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3C and is supported by experimental data.

claim: Nerve stimulation of P2ry1 mutants in the presence of the pan-cholinesterase inhibitor neostigmine results in a robust Ca2+ response in all TPSCs.
source: Nerve stimulation of P2ry1 mutants in the presence of the pan-cholinesterase inhibitor neostigmine resulted in a robust Ca2+ response in all TPSCs, suggesting that cholinesterase activity normally prevents this effect (n = 3; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments showing restoration of Ca2+ responses in P2ry1 mutants by neostigmine, as shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Cholinesterase activity normally prevents muscarinic-mediated Ca2+ responses in TPSCs during nerve stimulation.
source: Nerve stimulation of P2ry1 mutants in the presence of the pan-cholinesterase inhibitor neostigmine resulted in a robust Ca2+ response in all TPSCs, suggesting that cholinesterase activity normally prevents this effect (n = 3; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking cholinesterase with neostigmine allows muscarinic-mediated Ca2+ responses in P2ry1 mutants.

claim: Neostigmine increases the intensity of activity-induced Ca2+ transients in P2ry1 WT mice.
source: Neostigmine also increased the intensity of activity-induced Ca2+ transients in P2ry1 WT mice, demonstrating the additive nature of the effects of purinergic and muscarinic stimulation on this response (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing enhanced Ca2+ responses in WT mice treated with neostigmine, as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The effects of purinergic and muscarinic stimulation on TPSC Ca2+ responses are additive.
source: Neostigmine also increased the intensity of activity-induced Ca2+ transients in P2ry1 WT mice, demonstrating the additive nature of the effects of purinergic and muscarinic stimulation on this response (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that neostigmine enhances Ca2+ responses in WT mice that already have purinergic signaling.

claim: Bath application of either ATP or ADP induces Ca2+ responses in TPSCs.
source: While bath application of either ATP or ADP induced these responses, neither ADP-ribose nor β-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (βNAD) did (n = 4; data not shown; Mutafova-Yambolieva and Durnin, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of TPSC responses to different ligands.

claim: Neither ADP-ribose nor β-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (βNAD) induces Ca2+ responses in TPSCs.
source: While bath application of either ATP or ADP induced these responses, neither ADP-ribose nor β-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (βNAD) did (n = 4; data not shown; Mutafova-Yambolieva and Durnin, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of TPSC responses to different ligands.

claim: Bath application of the P1R-activating ligand adenosine evokes robust Ca2+ transients in TPSCs.
source: Bath application of the P1R-activating ligand adenosine also evoked robust Ca2+ transients in TPSCs (n = 3; data not shown), similar to previous studies (Robitaille, 1995; Castonguay and Robitaille, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and is consistent with previous studies (Robitaille, 1995; Castonguay and Robitaille, 2002).

claim: The onset of Ca2+ response to adenosine is markedly delayed compared to that triggered by purines or ACh mimetics (ATP = 3.2 ± 1.6 s, adenosine = 15.6 ± 3.4 s; p<0.001).
source: However, the onset of this response was markedly delayed, compared to that triggered by purines or ACh mimetics (ATP = 3.2 ± 1.6 s, adenosine = 15.6 ± 3.4 s; p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing onset times of Ca2+ responses to different ligands.

claim: Activity-induced Ca2+ signaling in neonatal diaphragm TPSCs is mediated by adenine nucleotide-mediated stimulation of P2Y1R.
source: Together, these pharmacological and genetic studies suggest that activity-induced Ca2+ signaling in neonatal diaphragm TPSCs is mediated by adenine nucleotide-mediated stimulation of P2Y1R.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the pharmacological and genetic experimental data presented in the preceding text.

claim: There is no difference in the total number of NMJs between P2ry1 mutant and WT mice at P7.
source: We found no difference in the total number of NMJs, the size of NMJs, the percentage of innervated NMJs, or the apposition of perisynaptic Schwann cells in P2ry1 mutant or WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of NMJ structure, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no difference in the size of NMJs between P2ry1 mutant and WT mice at P7.
source: We found no difference in the total number of NMJs, the size of NMJs, the percentage of innervated NMJs, or the apposition of perisynaptic Schwann cells in P2ry1 mutant or WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of NMJ structure, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no difference in the percentage of innervated NMJs between P2ry1 mutant and WT mice at P7.
source: We found no difference in the total number of NMJs, the size of NMJs, the percentage of innervated NMJs, or the apposition of perisynaptic Schwann cells in P2ry1 mutant or WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of NMJ structure, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no difference in the apposition of perisynaptic Schwann cells between P2ry1 mutant and WT mice at P7.
source: We found no difference in the total number of NMJs, the size of NMJs, the percentage of innervated NMJs, or the apposition of perisynaptic Schwann cells in P2ry1 mutant or WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of NMJ structure, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no difference in AChE expression or synaptic localization between P2ry1 mutant and WT mice at P7.
source: Using a highly specific antibody that fails to detect expression of this enzyme in AChE mutant mice, we were unable to observe any difference in its expression or synaptic localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis of AChE expression, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are no obvious structural abnormalities in NMJs of P2ry1 mutants as examined by electron microscopy.
source: Finally, we examined NMJs by electron microscopy, and found no obvious structural abnormalities (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy analysis of NMJ ultrastructure, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The gross morphological development of the NMJ, at least until P7 in the diaphragm, is unaffected in mice lacking P2Y1R and activity-induced Ca2+ signaling.
source: Together, these results suggest that the gross morphological development of the NMJ, at least until P7 in the diaphragm, is unaffected in mice lacking P2Y1R and activity-induced Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the morphological and ultrastructural data presented in the preceding text.

claim: The resting membrane potential (RMP) is unchanged between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice (−68.5 ± 5.2 vs. −68.4 ± 3.3 mV; WT vs. mutant; p=0.46; n = 3, c = 13).
source: The resting membrane potential (RMP) was unchanged between genotypes (−68.5 ± 5.2 vs. −68.4 ± 3.3 mV; WT vs. mutant; p=0.46; WT vs. mutant; n = 3, c = 13), and was not significantly different after vs. before a nerve stimulation bout between genotypes (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of muscle cell resting membrane potential.

claim: The frequency of miniature EPPs (mEPPs) is unchanged between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice (resting frequency: 0.38 ± 0.15 vs. 0.46 ± 0.14 events/s; p=0.11).
source: The frequency, amplitude, rise to peak, and time to 50% decay of miniature EPPs (mEPPs) were also unchanged (resting frequency: 0.38 ± 0.15 vs. 0.46 ± 0.14 events/s; p=0.11; post-stimulation frequency: 1.57 ± 0.8 vs. 2.01 ± 0.8 events/s; p=0.15; amplitude: 2.52 ± 0.5 vs. 2.49 ± 0.6 mV; p=0.44; rise to peak: 3.76 ± 1.8 vs. 3.69 ± 2.7 ms; p=0.46; time to 50% decay: 5.83 ± 2.4 vs. 4.81 ± 1.8 ms; p=0.08; WT vs. mutant; n = 3, c = 13–19).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of mEPP properties.

claim: The amplitude of miniature EPPs (mEPPs) is unchanged between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice (2.52 ± 0.5 vs. 2.49 ± 0.6 mV; p=0.44).
source: The frequency, amplitude, rise to peak, and time to 50% decay of miniature EPPs (mEPPs) were also unchanged (resting frequency: 0.38 ± 0.15 vs. 0.46 ± 0.14 events/s; p=0.11; post-stimulation frequency: 1.57 ± 0.8 vs. 2.01 ± 0.8 events/s; p=0.15; amplitude: 2.52 ± 0.5 vs. 2.49 ± 0.6 mV; p=0.44; rise to peak: 3.76 ± 1.8 vs. 3.69 ± 2.7 ms; p=0.46; time to 50% decay: 5.83 ± 2.4 vs. 4.81 ± 1.8 ms; p=0.08; WT vs. mutant; n = 3, c = 13–19).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of mEPP properties.

claim: Individual nerve-evoked EPPs are similar between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice.
source: Individual nerve-evoked EPPs, recorded in the presence of μ-conotoxin, were also similar between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of EPPs, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EPP amplitudes at the end of HFS are similar between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice.
source: In response to HFS, EPP amplitudes at the end of the period were also similar in each genotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of EPPs during HFS.

claim: Basal and HFS-induced ACh release are not affected in the absence of activity-induced Ca2+ signaling in TPSCs.
source: These results demonstrate that basal and HFS-induced ACh release are not affected in the absence of activity-induced Ca2+ signaling in TPSCs (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the electrophysiological data showing no differences in EPPs between genotypes.

claim: AChE expression at the NMJ is unaffected in P2ry1 mutants.
source: These results also corroborate the finding that AChE expression at the NMJ was unaffected in P2ry1 mutants, as the durations of mEPPs and EPPs were unaffected, whereas they are longer in the absence of this enzyme (Adler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mEPP and EPP durations are normal in P2ry1 mutants, combined with knowledge that these durations are longer in the absence of AChE (Adler et al., 2011).

claim: There is no difference in the amplitudes of basal muscle APs between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice (67.7 ± 7.1 vs. 67.8 ± 7.1 mV; p=0.49).
source: There was no difference in the amplitudes (67.7 ± 7.1 vs. 67.8 ± 7.1 mV; p=0.49), the rise to peak (1.16 ± 0.2 vs. 1.07 ± 0.2 ms; p=0.33), or the time to 50% decay (2.42 ± 0.53 vs. 2.16 ± 0.82 ms; p=0.43) of basal APs, or in the percentage of successfully transmitted muscle APs at the end of a period of HFS (note the three successful APs in the WT and 2 APs in the mutant, at the end of HFS; arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of muscle AP properties.

claim: There is no difference in the rise to peak of basal muscle APs between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice (1.16 ± 0.2 vs. 1.07 ± 0.2 ms; p=0.33).
source: There was no difference in the amplitudes (67.7 ± 7.1 vs. 67.8 ± 7.1 mV; p=0.49), the rise to peak (1.16 ± 0.2 vs. 1.07 ± 0.2 ms; p=0.33), or the time to 50% decay (2.42 ± 0.53 vs. 2.16 ± 0.82 ms; p=0.43) of basal APs, or in the percentage of successfully transmitted muscle APs at the end of a period of HFS (note the three successful APs in the WT and 2 APs in the mutant, at the end of HFS; arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of muscle AP properties.

claim: There is no difference in the time to 50% decay of basal muscle APs between P2ry1 WT and mutant mice (2.42 ± 0.53 vs. 2.16 ± 0.82 ms; p=0.43).
